pharm: Competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol biosynthesis, lowering intracellular cholesterol and upregulating LDL receptors to increase clearance of LDL-cholesterol from plasma. Hydrophilic statin with relatively hepatoselective uptake and minimal CYP450 metabolism.
quick: 40 mg once daily (range 10-80 mg); start 40 mg, titrate to lipid goal
May be taken with or without food, at any time of day
Contraindicated - discontinue when pregnancy recognized (cholesterol needed for fetal development)
Contraindicated - do not breastfeed during therapy
Significant impairment: start 10 mg once daily and titrate cautiously
Contraindicated in active liver disease or unexplained persistent transaminase elevations
Limit alcohol; heavy use raises risk of hepatotoxicity
Lipid panel, liver enzymes at baseline/as indicated, CK if myopathy symptoms
summary: Pravastatin sodium is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor used to lower total and LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. It is indicated for primary and secondary prevention of coronary events and for hyperlipidemias including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. Unlike lipophilic statins it is hydrophilic, is not appreciably metabolized by CYP3A4, and has a comparatively low potential for drug interactions, though myopathy/rhabdomyolysis remains a class risk especially with gemfibrozil, niacin, and other interacting drugs. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, lactation, and active liver disease. Therapy is given once daily with or without food and combined with diet and lifestyle measures.
indications: Reduction of risk of myocardial infarction, coronary revascularization, and cardiovascular mortality in hyperlipidemic patients (primary prevention)
Secondary prevention of cardiovascular events in patients with established coronary heart disease
Primary hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia (Fredrickson Types IIa and IIb) as an adjunct to diet
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia in adults and in pediatric patients 8 years and older
Hypertriglyceridemia (Type IV) and primary dysbetalipoproteinemia (Type III) inadequately responding to diet

dosage.d: 40 mg once daily; starting range 10-40 mg, may increase to 80 mg once daily
dosage.n: Titrate at 4-week intervals to lipid goal; lowest effective dose

dosage.d: Start 10 mg once daily at bedtime; do not exceed 20 mg/day

dosage.n: Doses >20 mg not studied in this age group

admin: Place patient on a standard cholesterol-lowering diet before and during therapy
May be taken with or without food, as a single dose at any time of day
When given with a bile-acid resin, dose pravastatin at least 1 hour before or 4 hours after the resin
Counsel patient to report unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially with malaise or fever
moa: Pravastatin is a competitive inhibitor of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the enzyme that catalyzes the rate-limiting conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, an early step in cholesterol biosynthesis. By reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis it depletes the intracellular cholesterol pool, which upregulates cell-surface LDL receptors and enhances uptake and catabolism of circulating LDL. Hepatic synthesis of VLDL, the LDL precursor, is also reduced. The net effect is lowering of total cholesterol, LDL-C, apolipoprotein B, and triglycerides, with a modest increase in HDL-C. Pravastatin is relatively hydrophilic and hepatoselective, and unlike several other statins it is not extensively metabolized by cytochrome P450 3A4.

absolute: Pregnancy and women who may become pregnant
Active liver disease or unexplained persistent elevations of serum transaminases
Known hypersensitivity to pravastatin or any component
relative: Heavy alcohol use or history of liver disease
Concomitant drugs that increase myopathy risk (gemfibrozil, niacin, cyclosporine, colchicine)
Predisposing factors for rhabdomyolysis (advanced age, renal impairment, hypothyroidism)
monitor: Creatine kinase if muscle symptoms occur
Glucose/HbA1c (statins may modestly raise blood glucose)

preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy. Cholesterol and products of cholesterol biosynthesis are essential for fetal development, and there is no benefit to maternal lipid lowering during pregnancy. Discontinue pravastatin as soon as pregnancy is recognized. Women of childbearing potential should use effective contraception.
lact: Contraindicated during breastfeeding. A small amount of pravastatin is excreted in human milk, and because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the nursing infant from interference with lipid metabolism, women taking pravastatin should not breastfeed.
renal: In patients with significant renal impairment, a starting dose of 10 mg once daily is recommended, with cautious titration. Renal impairment is also a predisposing factor for myopathy with statin therapy.
hepatic: Contraindicated in active liver disease or unexplained persistent transaminase elevations. Use with caution in patients who consume substantial amounts of alcohol or have a history of liver disease. Persistent increases in transaminases (>3x ULN) warrant dose reduction or discontinuation.

major: Gemfibrozil - markedly increases risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis; avoid combination
Cyclosporine - increases pravastatin exposure and myopathy risk; cap pravastatin at 20 mg/day
Other fibrates and niacin (lipid-modifying doses) - additive myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk
Colchicine - cases of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis when combined
moderate: Clarithromycin - increases pravastatin exposure; do not exceed 40 mg/day
Bile-acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol) - reduce pravastatin absorption; separate dosing
minor: Pravastatin is not significantly metabolized by CYP3A4, so it has fewer CYP-mediated interactions than lipophilic statins
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food does not clinically affect efficacy.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol intake; chronic heavy alcohol use increases the risk of hepatotoxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause elevations in liver transaminases and creatine kinase; statins can modestly raise fasting glucose and HbA1c.

serious: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury
emergency: Severe muscle pain/weakness with dark urine (rhabdomyolysis)
Signs of liver injury (jaundice, RUQ pain)

monitoring: Lipid panel before therapy and periodically to assess response
Liver function tests at baseline and when clinically indicated
Creatine kinase if muscle symptoms develop
Assess for muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness at each visit
counsel: Take once a day, with or without food, at the same time each day
Keep following a low-cholesterol diet and exercise plan while on this medicine
Tell your doctor right away about unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you also feel unwell or feverish
Do not take if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding - tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant
Report yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, or upper-abdominal pain
Limit alcohol and tell your doctor about all other medicines you take
pk: Lipid lowering begins within 1-2 weeks; maximal response in ~4 weeks
Plasma Tmax ~1-1.5 hours after oral dosing
Store at controlled room temperature 20-25 C; protect from moisture
pearls: Hydrophilic statin not metabolized by CYP3A4 - fewer azole/macrolide interactions than simvastatin or atorvastatin
Can be dosed at any time of day, not just bedtime, since lipid response is sustained
Avoid combination with gemfibrozil; cap dose with cyclosporine (20 mg) and clarithromycin (40 mg)
Routine periodic LFT monitoring is no longer required for all statins; check when clinically indicated
Stop and check CK for any unexplained muscle pain - consider immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy if symptoms persist after stopping
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take the next one at the regular time. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: There is no specific treatment for pravastatin overdose. Manage symptomatically and institute supportive measures as required. Monitor liver function and creatine kinase. Because pravastatin is highly protein bound, hemodialysis is not expected to substantially enhance clearance.
